0.title: Perspectives on AI and Analytics
0.content: If you are interested in how data science and AI actually get built in the real world — where business constraints, data quality, and operating models matter as much as modeling technique — this is the place to start. I write about the gap between the polished story of AI and the practical work of producing reliable, explainable, and operationally useful systems. Recent Essays . | Beyond the Agent Illusion: Leveraging AI Systems for Real Operational Value A comparison of two ways to build intelligent systems: the AI-first, agentic view and the data-science view. The essay argues that while there are niches such as self-driving cars and robotics where the agentic approach is essential, most enterprise operations are better served by the data-science view when decisions must be explained, trusted, and understood by business operators. | Data Scientist vs ML Engineer A practical look at the different responsibilities of data scientists and machine learning engineers, where their work overlaps, and how both roles contribute to building reliable systems that create operational value. | From Business Use Case to Technical Implementation Turning business problems into tractable analytical systems, with attention to constraints, data realities, and measurable outcomes. | From Task-Specific Data to Modeling How raw operational data becomes the modeling substrate, and why task framing matters as much as the algorithm. | Modeling and Featurization The design choices that shape model quality, especially where feature engineering determines whether the system captures signal or noise. | Why using AI to understand technical content needs care and deliberation Why generative AI can flatten nuanced technical material if it is treated as a substitute for careful reading and domain judgment. | tseda: Analyst-Guided Time-Series Decomposition — An open Python package for decomposing operational time series into interpretable components such as trend, seasonality, and noise, with explicit, repeatable, and reviewable diagnostics. | . These essays are intended to be practical, opinionated, and grounded in applied analytics rather than hype. They sit alongside the consulting and methodology work on this site, and they are meant to help teams think more clearly about where data science adds value and where it does not.

2.doc: Open, Client-Owned Analytics for Operational Decisions
2.title: Statistical Learning Built for the Real Decision
2.content: I help CTOs, engineering leaders, and operational teams turn organizational data into analytical systems that produce reliable, explainable, and maintainable decisions. R2-DS combines established statistical learning methods—refined by researchers and practitioners over decades—with disciplined software engineering. The result is a reusable, auditable solution that your organization can inspect, operate, extend, and own. Many analytics initiatives fail not because the team lacks algorithms, but because the solution does not adequately reflect the business process, data structure, validation requirements, or operational consequences. I focus on those gaps: problem framing, feature design, model selection, validation, monitoring, and maintenance. Foundation models and advanced techniques can be useful, but reinventing established methods is unnecessary when the available data and domain knowledge support a simpler, more transparent solution. 3.doc: Open, Client-Owned Analytics for Operational Decisions
3.title: Where the Approach Creates Value
3.content: Simply passing cleaned data to an algorithm rarely produces a robust operational system. Real data may contain imbalance, hidden subpopulations, correlated features, inconsistent semantics, and changing operating conditions. The useful question is not “Which algorithm should we run?” but: . | What decision must the model support? | What structure and limitations exist in the data? | Which signals are relevant to the business process? | How will success be measured in operation? | What will reveal that the assumptions are no longer valid? | . The SBA Loan Analytics example illustrates the difference. A broad feature set produced weak discrimination and required review of the full population. Applying disciplined feature selection and validation changed the result materially. The validation PR-AUC increased from 0.1673 to 0.7560. On held-out data, the resulting policy captured 82.46% of defaults while reviewing 19.55% of the population. This is not merely a better benchmark. It is a practical review queue aligned with an operational constraint. The same discipline applies in other settings. The Olist supply chain use case in kmds_migration is a second representative example. There, the challenge is not simply to predict an outcome, but to understand where delays, fulfillment risk, or customer-impacting issues emerge across sellers, products, and delivery flows, and to turn that understanding into an operational intervention that can be monitored, explained, and improved over time. The point is not to fit a model to data in isolation, but to design a decision-support system that reflects the business process and the operational realities it must serve. These examples are representative rather than exhaustive. If you have questions about a specific modeling task, get in touch. The full performance report and technical overview show how the result was constructed and evaluated.

4.doc: Open, Client-Owned Analytics for Operational Decisions
4.title: How I Help
4.content: 1. Frame the Real Problem . I translate an operational concern into explicit statistical tasks, decision criteria, and validation requirements. The work begins with the process generating the data—not with a preferred model or platform. 2. Build the Analytical Architecture . I identify relevant features, data structures, sources of heterogeneity, candidate models, and failure conditions. The objective is to create a defensible architecture that reflects the actual decision and can be explained to technical and business stakeholders. 3. Make the Solution Reproducible . The solution is implemented as a structured, versioned workflow. Data preparation, feature definitions, modeling decisions, validation results, and deployment requirements remain visible and recoverable rather than residing in an individual notebook or vendor environment. 4. Keep It Honest in Operation . A model can deteriorate when the underlying process changes. Monitoring includes performance, data drift, feature stability, concept drift, and the continuing validity of the business assumptions. When change is detected, the response is explicit: recalibrate, redesign, or retire the affected component.

5.doc: Open, Client-Owned Analytics for Operational Decisions
5.title: Open Tools, Client Ownership
5.content: The underlying components are open source and designed for reuse: . | KMDS provides a structured, reproducible workflow for analytical projects, including documented decisions, reusable project components, and agent-assisted execution. | Imbalanced Feature Screener identifies discriminative features in imbalanced datasets, supporting focused feature contracts where rare outcomes make conventional screening unreliable. | tseda supports analyst-guided time-series decomposition with explicit statistical traceability. | Count TS Window Selector selects a homogeneous Poisson-process window from a time series of arrivals, helping teams distinguish stable operating periods from regime changes. | Structure Identification for CS Data helps expose hidden dependencies, segmentation, and changes in datasets before they distort modeling results. | . The same workflow can support different business domains while retaining the discipline around data understanding, feature engineering, modeling, validation, and maintenance. Your organization retains the code, configuration, documentation, and analytical logic.

6.doc: Open, Client-Owned Analytics for Operational Decisions
6.title: A Practical Approach to AI
6.content: Agentic tools are used throughout the work to accelerate exploration, implementation, documentation, and repetitive engineering. They do not replace expert accountability. Human judgment remains responsible for defining the decision, recognizing misleading patterns, selecting appropriate validation, and deciding whether a result is ready for operational use. The same principle applies to foundation models. They can provide a useful baseline, support cold starts, or transfer patterns when there is strong repeated structure across tasks. They are not automatically preferable to a well-designed model trained on your own data. The right choice depends on business value, explainability, data characteristics, infrastructure, and maintenance cost. See Foundation Models for Tabular Data for a fuller discussion.

7.doc: Open, Client-Owned Analytics for Operational Decisions
7.title: Ways to Engage
7.content: Analytical Systems Audit — 2 to 3 Weeks . For a team that has data or an existing model but is uncertain why results are weak, unstable, or difficult to trust, the audit can include: . | Mapping the operational decision and expected business impact | Reviewing data structure, feature definitions, and sources of risk | Assessing class imbalance, heterogeneity, leakage, drift, and validation | Benchmarking the current approach against credible alternatives | Identifying the highest-value corrective actions | Delivering a prioritized architecture and implementation roadmap | . The audit is intended to give decision-makers a clear answer: what is failing, why it is failing, and what should be done next. Solution Development Kickoff . For a defined opportunity, the next step can be a focused solution kickoff covering the problem definition, statistical design, reproducibility structure, feature strategy, evaluation plan, and first implementation backlog. The engagement is structured around a durable capability rather than a disposable proof of concept. R2-DS works with U.S. enterprises and global capability centers (GCCs), including teams in Chennai and Bengaluru. Engagements can be structured through a direct independent-contractor agreement or a corporation-to-corporation arrangement, subject to the requirements of the parties.

11.title: Open-Platform Advisory Methodology
11.content: I help organizations build and maintain analytical systems around operational business data using a disciplined open-platform framework. The objective is not to rent a software stack; it is to design the statistical architecture, preserve the analytical knowledge that makes the system durable, and maintain model validity as the operating environment evolves. The Open-Platform Advisory Framework . | Map the operational process and decision cadence to a well-posed statistical problem. | Analyze the current datasets, quality issues, and operational constraints. | Design a maintainable analytical structure using open, auditable frameworks such as KMDS and tseda. | Build reusable feature engineering components that remain inside the client organization. | Diagnose drift, concept changes, and structural degradation before they produce bad decisions. | Preserve analytical knowledge for repeatable execution and long-term maintenance. | . Engagement Phases . | Initial Solution Mapping — Define the problem, entities, features, and model framing. | Drift & Gap Analysis — Evaluate whether the underlying assumptions still hold as the data-generating process changes. | Remediation & Calibration — Rebuild the feature definitions, decomposition windows, and model assumptions when necessary. | Mathematical Maintenance — Sustain the analytical system after initial deployment. | . Step 1: Understand the Data . Questions: . | What is the unit of analysis? | What entities exist? | What temporal structure exists? | What is the baseline data quality? | Where are the drift signals likely to appear? | . Tools: . | Time-series diagnostics | Dataset profiling | Feature lineage review | . Step 2: Understand the Business Process . Questions: . | What decisions are being made? | What relationships matter? | What patterns are stable? | What assumptions are economically valuable to preserve? | . Tools: . | KMDS component analysis | Operational process mapping | Statistical dependency review | . Step 3: Build Analytical Assets . Questions: . | What features matter? | What models are appropriate? | What operational assumptions need to be explicit? | What is the maintenance plan when drift emerges? | . Tools: . | Featurization | Modeling governance | Open-source analytical implementation | . Step 4: Preserve and Maintain the Mathematical System . Questions: . | What was learned? | What assumptions were made? | How is the solution maintained over time? | Where is the model at risk of drifting from physical reality? | . Tools: . | KMDS | tseda | Drift analysis and calibration protocols | . Typical Engagement Outcomes . | A clear analytical architecture for the business problem | Reusable and auditable feature definitions | Explicit model assumptions and operational limits | Drift diagnosis and remediation plans | Durable knowledge ownership inside the client organization | . My consulting and methodological design experience spans the US, India, and Europe. For practical examples, explore the KMDS migration repository.
